researchIntro: Recent and landmark studies in plain English, with the caveats that matter for a rain-fed KC lawn. Several were done by K-State, a couple of hours west in a similar climate; those are flagged. Every citation was checked against its DOI.

local.name: MU Extension county offices
local.what: Soil tests (call ahead; the MU lab's regular test is $15 in 2026, plus any county handling fee), lawn and garden questions, and classes. Jackson, Clay, Platte and Cass counties each have an office; on the Kansas side, K-State Research and Extension county offices do the same.
local.where: Find your county's office on the MU Extension site

local.name: Master Gardeners of Greater KC: garden hotline
local.what: Free answers from trained volunteers. The 24-hour voicemail is answered in season; their site lists in-person help hours. Email mggkc.hotline@gmail.com. Soil-test drop-off info is on their site.

local.name: Kansas City Community Gardens
local.what: Income-based memberships with low-cost transplants (spring cool-season sale; "Tomato Days" in late April), seeds, classes and garden plots.

local.name: MDC tree seedlings (George O. White State Forest Nursery)
local.what: Inexpensive bare-root native trees and shrubs. Order Sep 1–Apr 15 by mail (Apr 30 online); shipping or pickup mid-February to mid-May.

local.name: Callery pear buyback (MDC & partners)
local.what: Cut down a Bradford/Callery pear, register with a photo, and pick up a free native tree. The 2026 event included a KC-area pickup site; watch for 2027 dates in early spring.

local.name: Missouri 811
local.what: Free utility locates before you dig. Missouri law requires at least 2 working days' notice; Missouri 811 says allow 3.

local.name: CoCoRaHS Missouri
local.what: Volunteer rain and snow reporting with a standard 4-inch gauge. Your reports help forecasters, and neighbors' reports help you.

local.name: Grow Native!
local.what: Missouri Prairie Foundation's native plant program: plant database, care calendar and a directory of nurseries that sell natives.

suppliers.name: Soil Service Garden Center
suppliers.what: Local tall fescue blends (**KC Endurance**, **KC Marathon** with 10% bluegrass), fertilizer, plants.

suppliers.name: Grass Pad
suppliers.where: Olathe, Lee's Summit, Kansas City (Barry Rd), Bonner Springs and Stilwell

suppliers.name: Family Tree Nursery
suppliers.what: Trees, shrubs, perennials, natives; knowledgeable staff.

suppliers.name: SiteOne Landscape Supply
suppliers.what: **LESCO** fertilizer (28-0-12, urea), certified seed (Kansas Excalibur), pro herbicides such as Stonewall prodiamine and Tenacity. Call the branch; some items are by request.

suppliers.name: Missouri Organic Recycling
suppliers.what: Bulk compost, mulch and soil blends, with delivery.

suppliers.name: Planters Seed & Spice Co.
suppliers.what: Historic River Market seed store: bulk vegetable and grass seed, onion sets, seed potatoes.

suppliers.name: Merriam Feed + Seed
suppliers.what: Grass seed by the pound, feed-store basics.

suppliers.name: Johnny's Selected Seeds
suppliers.what: Hybrid and organic vegetable seed, Agribon row cover, seed-starting gear (mail order).

suppliers.name: DoMyOwn
suppliers.what: Pro lawn products (Tenacity, Prodiamine 65 WDG, Dimension 2EW, SedgeHammer) in homeowner sizes.

suppliers.name: Home Depot / Lowe's / Ace
suppliers.what: Scotts, Ortho, BioAdvanced, Pennington, Preen, spreaders, sprinklers and timers; aerator rental.

myths.myth: Water the lawn a little every day in summer.
myths.fact: Daily sprinkles grow shallow roots and disease. Soak ½–1 in only when needed (the 3-week rule), early in the morning.

myths.myth: A brown lawn in August is dead.
myths.fact: Tall fescue goes dormant and recovers; in K-State trials it came back after 60–83 days with no water. Tug-test it before you panic.

myths.myth: Spring is the time to fertilize.
myths.fact: For tall fescue it's fall. In K-State plots, spring and May nitrogen went with 48–66% brown patch vs 2–23% for a September-only feeding.

myths.myth: A spring weed-and-feed takes care of everything.
myths.fact: Broadleaf weeds die best in fall, crabgrass preventer needs precise timing, and the lawn doesn't need April nitrogen. Combo products do each job at the wrong time.
Sand plus clay makes a concrete-like mix. Compost and core aeration are the fix.
Only in sodium-affected soils, which KC's generally aren't. Spend the money on compost instead.

myths.myth: Grub control gets rid of moles.
myths.fact: Moles eat mostly earthworms. Trapping is the reliable fix.

myths.myth: Japanese beetle traps protect my roses.
myths.fact: Traps attract far more beetles than they catch (University of Kentucky research; MU agrees). Hand-pick instead.

myths.myth: Blossom-end rot means the soil needs calcium (or Epsom salt).
myths.fact: Usually it's uneven watering; K-State says low soil calcium is rare in Kansas. Mulch, water evenly, and test before adding anything.

myths.myth: Rhizomatous tall fescue will fill in bare spots.
myths.fact: K-State measured RTF rhizomes at about 3 mm vs 80+ mm for bluegrass. Reseed bare spots.

myths.myth: No Mow May is proven to help bees.
myths.fact: The study behind it was retracted in 2022. Mowing every 2–3 weeks and planting flowers does help (Lerman 2018).
Only if the soil is acidic. MU says to lime lawns only at pH 5.8 or lower, so test first.

myths.myth: Bag the clippings to prevent thatch.
myths.fact: Clippings break down fast and return nitrogen; tall fescue rarely builds thatch.

myths.myth: Seed in spring and put down crabgrass preventer at the same time.
myths.fact: Most preventers stop grass seed too. Seed in September; in spring use only mesotrione (Tenacity) or siduron at seeding.
A 2024 study found no consistent drought benefit. Choose cultivars with good NTEP data instead.

myths.myth: KY-31 is just as good and cheaper.
myths.fact: It's a 1943 pasture grass: coarse and clumpy. It scored 4.4 in NTEP's 2018 test vs 6.3–6.4 for the best turf types.
Many consumer Roundup products no longer contain glyphosate, or contain only a little. Read the active ingredient on the label, not the brand name.

myths.myth: Mulch piled around a tree protects it.
myths.fact: Mulch against the trunk rots bark and invites rodents and girdling roots. Make a flat donut, 2–3 in deep.

creditsIntro: Several features were inspired by these public GitHub projects. We borrowed ideas only; all code on this site is original. Thank you to their authors.

credits.name: racoutlaw/gardening-guide (Plant by Frost)
credits.idea: Planting windows tied to frost dates, so setting your own frost dates shifts the whole plan; a "My garden" star list.

credits.name: baditaflorin/urban-farm-year
credits.idea: Static, offline-friendly GitHub Pages planner; versioned local-storage envelope; JSON backup/restore; Open-Meteo weather.

credits.name: gofjhmakit/gardentoolkit
credits.idea: iCal export; companion notes labeled by evidence level.

credits.name: gabrielcsapo/backyard-garden (Gardeneus)
credits.idea: Gantt-style planting timeline, weekly checklists, crop-rotation warnings within 3 years, harvest totals.

credits.name: alexwboles/gardenplan-ai
credits.idea: No-build, no-dependency app that saves to localStorage; an upcoming-tasks list.

credits.name: cmanorome/pd-application-calendar
credits.idea: A 12-month lawn product application calendar with rates and .ics export.

credits.name: lujoh/amper_garden_planner

dataCredits: Weather, soil temperature and evapotranspiration: [Open-Meteo](https://open-meteo.com/) (free, no key).
Climate normals and freeze probabilities: NOAA NCEI U.S. Climate Normals 1991–2020, Kansas City International Airport (USW00003947).
Planting dates: University of Missouri Extension G6201. Vegetable varieties: K-State Research and Extension L41.
Lawn cultivar data: National Turfgrass Evaluation Program (NTEP) 2018 National Tall Fescue Test.
Heading font: Fraunces by the Fraunces Project Authors (SIL Open Font License 1.1). Icons drawn for this site.
